---
title: "Sources worth getting as PDFs"
description: "The books and articles that would most improve the Rhythm Library, ranked by what they would unlock. Drop a PDF in Downloads and ask for the page to be updated from it."
---

These come from the gaps found while building the [Rhythm Library](../tools/rhythm-library.qmd) (November 2026): sources that
cards already lean on second-hand, or that would fill a gap listed under its "Not here yet" section. They are ranked
by impact. The most useful are those that would replace a weak source (an uncited Wikipedia list, a notes website) or let
a pattern go on the page at all.

**Got (27 Nov 2026), now used on the site:** Kippen and Nelson (Garland vol. 5), Clayton, Wichmann, and Toussaint's book (rows 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 below). Garland vol. 5 also corrected the sitar, tanpura and raga pages. Still wanted: Peñalosa (row 3 and *Rumba Quinto*) and the rest.

## Highest impact

| # | Source | What it would unlock | Getting it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kippen, James. "Hindustani Tāla." *Garland Encyclopedia of World Music*, vol. 5, *South Asia*, ed. Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000. | A scholarly source for every Hindustani card, which now rests on Courtney's web pages and thin Wikipedia articles; settles the disputed tāls (chautāl, dhamār, rūpak's khālī sam); adds sūltāl, tilwāḍā. | The copy once posted as a UC Irvine course reading is gone; a library copy of vol. 5 or its PDF |
| 2 | Nelson, David. "Karnatak Tāla." Same volume. | The Carnatic section: hand actions for the chāpu tāḷas (now shown as groups only), and a better source than Wikipedia for the aṅgas, jātis and nadai. | As above |
| 3 | Peñalosa, David. *The Clave Matrix: Afro-Cuban Rhythm: Its Principles and African Origins*. Bembe Books, 2009. | The source behind most of Wikipedia's clave and bell-pattern material: the African 4/4 bells, the Abakuá bell, kadodo and afrekete grids (all image-only now). | Book (Bembe Books) |
| 4 | Clayton, Martin. *Time in Indian Music: Rhythm, Metre, and Form in North Indian Rāg Performance*. Oxford UP, 2000. | The standard study of Hindustani metre: theka and laya, how tāls are really kept. | Book |
| 5 | Wichmann, Elizabeth. *Listening to Theatre: The Aural Dimension of Beijing Opera*. U of Hawaii P, 1991. | Ban and yan and the banshi from a full source rather than tutorial slides and a dictionary; the percussion patterns (*luogu*), which the page now leaves out. | Book |
| 6 | Toussaint, Godfried. *The Geometry of Musical Rhythm: What Makes a "Good" Rhythm Good?* 2nd ed., CRC Press, 2019. | Box-notation grids for many timelines in one checked source (his two Bridges papers already give 26 of the cards). | Book |

## Also useful

| Source | What it would unlock | Getting it |
|---|---|---|
| Peñalosa, David. *Rumba Quinto*. Bembe Books, 2010, pp. 141-44. | Cáscara and the songo bell, both now image-only on Wikipedia. | Book |
| Quintana, José Luis "Changuito." *Changuito: A Master's Approach to Timbales*. Alfred, 1998. | Songo as its creator teaches it (Wikipedia's other songo source). | Book |
| Caro Repetto, Rafael. *The Musical Dimension of Chinese Traditional Theatre*. PhD thesis, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, 2018. | Banshi and shengqiang in detail. | Free: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2030599 (blocked from the network used here) |
| Srinivasamurthy, Ajay, et al. "Transcription and Recognition of Syllable Based Percussion Patterns: The Case of Beijing Opera." *Proc. ISMIR*, 2014, pp. 431-36. | The named jingju percussion patterns written as syllables. | Free on archives.ismir.net (blocked from the network used here) |
| Zhang, Shuo, Rafael Caro Repetto, and Xavier Serra. "Understanding the Expressive Functions of Jingju Metrical Patterns through Lyrics Text Mining." *Proc. ISMIR*, 2017, pp. 397-403. | What each banshi expresses, checked against a corpus. | Free (blocked here) |
| Lopes, Nei. *Partido-Alto: Samba de Bamba*. Pallas, 2005. | Partido alto from a Brazilian source; Wikipedia's grid has no citation. | Book (Portuguese) |

The "Free" items need no purchase: download them on another network and drop the PDF in Downloads.

A second-line drumming source is still missing. Wikipedia's article prints no rhythm and cites nothing for it, and no
book was named in what was read.
